**MEMORANDUM**

**To:** [Supervising Partner]
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 20, 2026
**Re:** Vailous Auto Remarketing Holdings, LLC / Acquisition of Stonebarrow Vehicle Auctions, Inc.: Buyer-Side Exposure in the Deal Documents
**Privileged & Confidential: Attorney Work Product**

---

## I. Bottom Line

I reviewed all nine documents in the folder:

- the signed Stock Purchase Agreement dated August 3, 2026 (the "SPA");
- the agreed-form IP Assignment Agreement, Bill of Sale, Seller Note, Escrow Agreement and Transition Services Agreement ("TSA");
- the Disclosure Schedule, including Supplement No. 1;
- the Hollenmere insurance certificate cover letter; and
- our client's September 29, 2026 objection letter.

The deal is for all shares of Stonebarrow Vehicle Auctions, Inc. (the "Company") for a **Purchase Price of $42,000,000** (SPA §2.1). Of that amount:

- $6,000,000 is deferred through the Seller Note; and
- $3,150,000 of the cash goes into the indemnity escrow.

Closing has not occurred, and the **Outside Date is December 18, 2026** (SPA §10.1(b)). That leaves roughly four weeks. All of the problems below can still be fixed before Closing, and the Outside Date gives both sides an incentive to agree. Any change to the signed SPA needs a written amendment signed by both parties (SPA §11.7). Changes to the agreed-form ancillaries need Seller's agreement to revised forms.

**Five issues need attention. They are listed in priority order:**

| # | Priority | Issue | Location |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Critical** | Uncapped Title and Odometer indemnity is routed into the TSA's three-month fee cap | SPA §9.8; TSA Sched. A (A-1) and §9.2 |
| 2 | **Critical** | Objection to Supplement No. 1 (Calloway odometer class action) was late, so the supplement may be deemed accepted | SPA §6.8; Disclosure Schedule, Supplement No. 1 cover statement; Buyer letter (Sept. 29, 2026) |
| 3 | **High** | General Representations survive only 90 days after Closing | SPA §9.1; Escrow Agreement §4.1 |
| 4 | **High** | Seller Note uses Delaware law and courts, which conflicts with the SPA's New York law and courts and splits off the setoff right | Seller Note §8; SPA §§9.7, 11.8, 11.9, 11.12 |
| 5 | **Medium–High** | TSA lets Pritouth assign or delegate to anyone, including a competitor | TSA §13.3 |

Issues 1 and 2 make each other worse. Both bear on the Calloway odometer class action, which is the largest known exposure in this deal. They should be negotiated together.

---

## II. Issues, Ranked

### Issue 1 (Critical): The Title and Odometer carve-out is undone by routing those claims to the TSA cap

**Where:**
- SPA §9.2(d) (Title and Odometer Losses)
- SPA §9.5(b) (carve-out from the cap)
- SPA §9.8 (Transition Services Matters)
- TSA Schedule A, Service A-1
- TSA §9.2 (Cap on Liability)
- TSA §10.1

**What the documents say:**
- **SPA §9.2(d)** gives Vailous a specific indemnity for title defects, title-brand nondisclosure and odometer misstatements on any vehicle sold through the Auctions **before Closing**. It applies "regardless of whether disclosed in the Disclosure Schedule."
- **SPA §9.5(b)** carves these "Title and Odometer Losses" out of the $210,000 basket and the $4,200,000 general cap. They are limited only by the Purchase Price.
- **SPA §9.8** then provides that "[a]ny Losses arising out of or relating to the subject matter of the Services shall be recovered exclusively under, and subject to the limitations of, the Transition Services Agreement."
- **TSA Schedule A, Service A-1** defines the Title Office Services as "title remediation, title transfer and odometer disclosure processing for all vehicles sold through the Auctions **before and after the Closing**." This expressly includes resolving defective-title and odometer exceptions, and announcing "not actual mileage" and odometer-discrepancy brands.
- **TSA §9.2** caps Provider's aggregate liability at "the Service Fees paid in the three (3) months preceding the event giving rise to the claim."

**Why it matters to Vailous:**
- Pre-Closing title and odometer problems are squarely "the subject matter of the Services." Seller will therefore argue that §9.8 pulls every Title and Odometer Loss out of the SPA and into the TSA.
  - The SPA's order-of-precedence clause (§11.12) does not help. There is no "conflict" between the documents, because the SPA itself sends these Losses to the TSA.
- Under the TSA, the recovery is very small:
  - Total monthly Service Fees under Schedule B are $103,000, so the best case is about **$309,000**.
  - The cap is measured by fees paid in the three months *before the event*. For a pre-Closing title or odometer event, no TSA fees had been paid at all, because the TSA only becomes effective at Closing (TSA §13.8). Seller can argue the cap is **$0**.
- TSA §10.1 indemnifies only third-party claims "caused by" Provider's breach, negligence or violation of law *in performing the Services*. Pre-Closing conduct of the Company is arguably not covered at all.
- The practical result is that the protection the SPA sets up as uncapped for this exact risk becomes worth between $0 and about $309,000.
- The Calloway putative nationwide class action seeks the greater of treble damages or $10,000 per violation under 49 U.S.C. §32710 for sales since January 2023. It is the single largest risk in the deal, and it sits squarely within this gap.

**Recommended fix (in order of preference):**
1. Amend SPA §9.8 to add: "provided that this Section 9.8 shall not apply to, and shall not limit, any Losses under Section 9.2(a), 9.2(b), 9.2(c) or 9.2(d), including Title and Odometer Losses, or any Losses arising from facts, events or conduct occurring on or before the Closing Date." Ideally, limit §9.8 to Losses caused by Provider's *post-Closing performance* of the Services.
2. Also revise TSA Schedule A, Service A-1, to cover only post-Closing processing. Strike "before and after the Closing." If pre-Closing title remediation must remain a service, state expressly that it does not shift or limit Seller's §9.2(d) indemnity.
3. As a backstop, add to TSA §9.2 that the cap does not apply to any matter that is also indemnifiable under the SPA, and that nothing in the TSA limits the SPA's Article IX.

---

### Issue 2 (Critical): Our objection to Supplement No. 1 was late, so Seller can argue the Calloway action is "cured"

**Where:**
- SPA §6.8 (Disclosure Schedule Supplements)
- Disclosure Schedule, Supplement No. 1, cover statement
- Buyer objection letter dated September 29, 2026

**What the documents say:**
- **SPA §6.8** provides that unless Buyer delivers a written objection "within ten (10) Business Days after receipt" of a Schedule Supplement, the supplement is "deemed accepted." The disclosed matters are then deemed to cure any related breach. That cure applies both to the §8.2 closing conditions *and* to Article IX indemnification.
- Supplement No. 1 adds the *Calloway Pre-Owned Motors v. Stonebarrow* odometer class action (S.D.N.Y.) to §4.13. It also adds a blanket liability item to §4.5 and cross-references §4.10.
- The cover statement says it was **delivered to Buyer on September 8, 2026** (a Tuesday) by email to Buyer's notice address, with a courier copy, under SPA §11.3.
- Ten Business Days from September 8 runs to **Tuesday, September 22, 2026**:
  - September 9–11 are days 1–3.
  - September 14–18 are days 4–8.
  - September 21–22 are days 9–10.
  - There are no intervening bank holidays.
- Our letter is dated **September 29, 2026**. It was **one week late.**

**Why it matters to Vailous:**
- Seller can take the position that Calloway is deemed accepted. On that view, Vailous:
  - could not rely on Calloway to refuse to close under §8.2(a) (the bring-down of §§4.5, 4.10 and 4.13); and
  - would have no §9.2(a) indemnity claim for breach of those representations.
- The September 29 letter disputes the supplement and reserves rights, so the client has not acquiesced. However, the letter does not cure the timing problem.
- We do have arguments, but none is a sure thing:
  - **(a) Scope of §6.8.** Section 6.8 permits supplements only for matters "arising or first becoming known to Seller after the date of this Agreement." The underlying conduct dates back to January 2023, so the supplement arguably falls outside §6.8 altogether. Our letter makes this point.
  - **(b) Section 9.2(d) is unaffected.** Section 9.2(d) indemnifies Title and Odometer Losses "regardless of whether disclosed," so the deemed-cure should not touch that specific indemnity.
- Argument (b) only works if Issue 1 is fixed. Otherwise §9.8 routes those Losses to the TSA cap. Taken together, Issues 1 and 2 could leave Vailous with almost no recourse for Calloway.
- Note also:
  - The Company's response to the complaint was due October 22, 2026. We should confirm its status.
  - The carrier has not issued a coverage position. The Hollenmere letter shows the E&O policy, which covers title and odometer E&O, has a $3,000,000 aggregate limit. That is likely insufficient against statutory damages on a class basis.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Before Closing, obtain a written amendment or waiver signed by Seller under SPA §11.7 that:
   - treats the September 29 letter as a timely objection; and
   - provides that Supplement No. 1 does not cure any breach for purposes of §8.2 or Article IX.
2. In addition, or if Seller resists, obtain a **special, uncapped, first-dollar indemnity** for all Losses arising from the Calloway action and the underlying conduct. It should be:
   - outside the basket and cap;
   - outside the reach of §9.8; and
   - backed by a dedicated escrow or holdback, sized with litigation counsel's input, that does not release until Calloway is finally resolved.
3. Keep the leverage points in view:
   - Buyer's reserved §8.2 condition arguments;
   - the §6.8 scope argument; and
   - the December 18 Outside Date.
4. Confirm that Seller has agreed not to settle or stipulate to class certification without Buyer's consent, as requested in the September 29 letter.
5. Process point: calendar all future supplement deadlines from the date of receipt under §11.3. Consider asking Seller to delete or soften the deemed-acceptance mechanism in §6.8 for any further supplements.

---

### Issue 3 (High): General Representations survive only 90 days after Closing

**Where:**
- SPA §9.1 (Survival)
- SPA §1.1 (definition of "Escrow Release Date")
- Escrow Agreement §4.1

**What the documents say:**
- **SPA §9.1** provides that the General Representations "shall survive the Closing until the Escrow Release Date."
- The SPA does not define that term. It defers to the Escrow Agreement (SPA §1.1).
- **Escrow Agreement §4.1** defines it as "ninety (90) days after the Closing Date."
- Under SPA §9.1, no claim may be brought once the survival period ends, unless written notice was given beforehand.

**Why it matters to Vailous:**
- The General Representations are every Article IV representation other than the Fundamental Representations and Taxes. They include the representations most likely to produce post-Closing claims:
  - financial statements (§4.4);
  - undisclosed liabilities (§4.5);
  - Consignor Funds trust handling (§4.6);
  - dealer and auction Licenses (§4.7);
  - auction receivables (§4.8);
  - floorplan arrangements (§4.9);
  - title and odometer compliance (§4.10);
  - material contracts (§4.11); and
  - litigation (§4.13).
- A 90-day window:
  - ends before a full audit cycle and before the first year-end close;
  - is too short to surface consignor shortfalls, floorplan lender disputes or license problems;
  - coincides with Buyer's own 90-day deadline for the closing statement under SPA §2.4; and
  - ends while Vailous is still relying on Pritouth for accounting and consignor reconciliation under TSA Service A-4.
- Once the window closes, the $3,150,000 escrow is released to Seller (Escrow §4.2). The $4,200,000 general cap then becomes practically worthless.
- The SPA's precedence clause (§11.12) does not fix this. There is no conflict between the documents: the SPA simply adopts the Escrow Agreement's date.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Amend SPA §9.1 to give the General Representations a stand-alone survival period of **at least 15–18 months after Closing**, with no cross-reference to the escrow. Eighteen months covers a full audit cycle.
2. Conform Escrow Agreement §4.1 so the Escrow Release Date matches. A partial step-down release at 12 months is an acceptable fallback.
3. Consider carving §4.6 (Consignor Funds) and §4.7 (Licenses) into a longer survival tier.

---

### Issue 4 (High): The Seller Note's Delaware law and forum conflict with the SPA's New York law and forum and threaten the setoff right

**Where:**
- Seller Note §8.1 and §8.2
- SPA §9.7 (Right of Setoff)
- SPA §11.8 (Governing Law)
- SPA §11.9 (Submission to Jurisdiction)
- SPA §11.12 (Order of Precedence)
- SPA §1.1 (definition of "Ancillary Agreements")

**What the documents say:**
- **SPA §§11.8–11.9** select **New York law** and the **exclusive** jurisdiction of state and federal courts in New York County.
- **SPA §9.7** lets Buyer set off indemnifiable Losses "against any payments due under the Seller Note." It also states that a good-faith setoff "shall not constitute a default under the Seller Note."
- **Seller Note §8.1** selects the **laws of the State of Delaware**.
- **Seller Note §8.2** requires any dispute "arising out of or relating to this Note" to be brought **exclusively** in Delaware courts in New Castle County, or in the U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware.
- **SPA §11.12** provides that the SPA prevails over the "Ancillary Agreements." Both §11.12 and the §1.1 definition limit that term to the Escrow Agreement, TSA, IP Assignment Agreement and Bill of Sale. **The Seller Note is not included.** The precedence clause therefore does *not* resolve this conflict.
- The Note itself:
  - contains no setoff provision;
  - treats non-payment of principal or interest as an Event of Default after 10 Business Days' notice (§6.1(a)); and
  - allows acceleration, default interest and collection costs (§§2.3, 6.2, 6.3).

**Why it matters to Vailous:**
- The $6,000,000 Note is Vailous's most practical source of recovery once the escrow is gone. This is especially true if Issue 3 is not fixed.
- Suppose Vailous withholds a Note payment under §9.7. Pritouth can then sue on the Note in Delaware, under Delaware law. It can argue that:
  - the Note is a separate instrument with no setoff right; and
  - the SPA's statement that setoff is not a default does not bind a Delaware court applying the Note.
- Vailous would then have to litigate its New York-law indemnity claims in New York while defending acceleration in Delaware. The likely results are:
  - competing exclusive-forum clauses;
  - parallel proceedings and inconsistent results; and
  - pressure to pay the Note and chase the indemnity separately.

**Recommended fix:**
1. **Preferred:** Revise the agreed-form Note before it is issued at Closing:
   - conform §8 to New York law and exclusive New York County courts, matching SPA §§11.8–11.9; and
   - add an express setoff clause in the Note mirroring SPA §9.7, including the statement that a good-faith setoff is not a default under §6.1.
2. **Also, or as a fallback:** Amend SPA §1.1 and §11.12 to add the Seller Note to "Ancillary Agreements," so the SPA prevails over any inconsistent term in the Note.
3. Make sure any Subordination Agreement with the Senior Lender does not override the setoff right.

---

### Issue 5 (Medium–High): Pritouth may assign or delegate the TSA to anyone, including a competitor

**Where:** TSA §13.3 (Assignment and Delegation)

**What the documents say:**
- Provider "may assign this Agreement, or delegate or subcontract the performance of any Services, in whole or in part, to any Person without the consent of Recipient."
- Recipient (the Company) may not assign without Provider's consent.

**Why it matters to Vailous:**
- Under the TSA, Pritouth will handle the Company's most sensitive functions and data, including:
  - title files and odometer statements;
  - consignor, buying-dealer, bidder and floorplan-lender data;
  - daily Consignor Funds trust reconciliation; and
  - access management for LaneLink and the simulcast systems.
- Pritouth could transfer all of this, together with the data access, to a rival wholesale auction operator or an unvetted subcontractor, and the Company would have no say.
- The protections in place would not stop that:
  - The data-use restrictions in TSA §7.1 bind "Provider," and their practical value against a downstream assignee is uncertain.
  - The SPA's non-compete and non-solicit (§6.6) expressly exempt activity "in the performance of the Services."
  - The SPA's non-compete and confidentiality covenants (§§6.5–6.6) bind Seller and its Affiliates, not an unaffiliated assignee.
- The provision is also one-sided compared with the IP Assignment Agreement (§5.3), where Pritouth cannot assign without the Company's consent.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Revise TSA §13.3 so that neither party may assign or delegate without the other's prior written consent. Allow a narrow exception for Recipient to assign to Buyer's Affiliates or successors.
2. Add an express prohibition on any assignment, delegation or subcontracting to a Person that, directly or through Affiliates, operates a wholesale vehicle auction or competing remarketing business.
3. Require that:
   - any approved subcontractor be bound in writing by TSA §7 and by the equivalent of SPA §§6.5–6.6; and
   - Provider remain fully liable for its subcontractors.

---

## III. Other Observations (Lower Priority)

- **Order of precedence.** SPA §11.12 provides that the SPA prevails over the Ancillary Agreements (Escrow Agreement, TSA, IP Assignment Agreement and Bill of Sale) if there is a conflict. As noted above:
  - it does not reach the Seller Note (Issue 4); and
  - it does not cure Issues 1 or 3, because in each case the SPA itself imports the problematic term.
- **Escrow sizing.** The $3,150,000 escrow is below the $4,200,000 general cap and is the first source of recovery for General Representation claims (SPA §9.6). Given Calloway, consider asking for a larger escrow or a separate Calloway holdback (see Issue 2).
- **Insurance (Hollenmere letter, Oct. 14, 2026).**
  - Several policies are written on Seller's combined account and carry change-of-control provisions.
  - Buyer is not an additional insured.
  - Coordinate replacement or endorsement of the program effective at Closing, and confirm that the E&O carrier's coverage position on Calloway is preserved after Closing.
- **Licenses.**
  - The Connecticut Wholesale Dealer License expires December 31, 2026 (Disclosure Schedule §4.7, Part C). Confirm the November renewal was filed.
  - The change-of-control filings and bond riders listed in Schedule §4.3 must be complete to satisfy SPA §8.1(b) and §8.2(d) by the Outside Date.
- **Bill of Sale and IP Assignment.** I found no material issues. Both use New York law and forum, consistent with the SPA, and route claims through SPA Article IX.

---

## IV. Recommended Next Steps

1. Send Seller a single issues list and markup covering:
   - SPA amendments to §§1.1, 6.8, 9.1, 9.8 and 11.12, plus a Calloway special indemnity and holdback;
   - a revised Escrow Agreement §4.1;
   - a revised Seller Note §8, with a setoff clause; and
   - revised TSA Schedule A, §9.2 and §13.3.
2. Present Issues 1 and 2 together as a package on the Calloway exposure. That gives us the strongest leverage.
3. Bring in litigation counsel to estimate Calloway exposure for sizing the holdback. Obtain the information requested in our September 29 letter if it has not yet been produced.
4. Track the December 18, 2026 Outside Date. If Seller will not agree to the Calloway protections, preserve the client's position under §§8.2(a), 8.2(c) and 10.1.

Please let me know if you would like me to prepare the markups.

# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 20, 2026
**Re:** Vailous Auto Remarketing Holdings, LLC / Acquisition of Stonebarrow Vehicle Auctions, Inc.: Buyer-side exposure in the deal documents

---

## I. Summary

On August 3, 2026, Vailous Auto Remarketing Holdings, LLC ("**Vailous**" or "**Buyer**") signed a Stock Purchase Agreement (the "**SPA**") with Pritouth Dealer Services, Inc. ("**Pritouth**" or "**Seller**"). Under it, Vailous will acquire all shares of Stonebarrow Vehicle Auctions, Inc. (the "**Company**") for a **Purchase Price of $42,000,000** (SPA §2.1). The price is paid as follows:

- **$6,000,000** is deferred through a subordinated Seller Note (SPA §1.1; Note §1.1).
- **$3,150,000** of the cash goes into an indemnity escrow with Cindral Trust Company, N.A. (Escrow Agreement §2.1).

Closing has not occurred. The **Outside Date is December 18, 2026** (SPA §10.1(b)), which is four weeks away. Each fix below needs Pritouth's agreement, and we have leverage until Closing.

I reviewed all nine documents in the folder:

- the SPA
- the IP Assignment Agreement
- the Bill of Sale
- the Disclosure Schedule, including Supplement No. 1
- the Seller Note
- the Escrow Agreement
- the Transition Services Agreement (the "**TSA**")
- the Hollenmere insurance certificate cover letter
- Vailous's September 29, 2026 objection letter

The Bill of Sale and the insurance cover letter raise no substantive issues for Buyer beyond the routine change-of-control insurance placement noted in Part III.

**Background point on precedence.** SPA §11.12 provides that **the SPA prevails over the Ancillary Agreements** if they conflict. SPA §1.1 and §11.12 define the Ancillary Agreements as only four documents: the Escrow Agreement, the TSA, the IP Assignment Agreement and the Bill of Sale. **The Seller Note is not on that list.** This gap matters for Issue 3 below.

### Priority overview

| # | Priority | Issue | Location |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **High** | Late objection to Supplement No. 1 (odometer class action may be deemed accepted and cured) | SPA §6.8; Disclosure Schedule, Supplement No. 1 cover statement; Buyer letter (Sept. 29, 2026) |
| 2 | **High** | General Representations survive only 90 days after Closing | SPA §9.1; Escrow Agreement §4.1 |
| 3 | **High** | Seller Note chooses Delaware law and forum, against the SPA's New York choices; this threatens Buyer's setoff | Seller Note §8; SPA §§9.7, 11.8, 11.9, 11.12 |
| 4 | **Medium** | Pritouth may assign or delegate the TSA to anyone, including a competitor | TSA §13.3 |
| 5 | Low | Housekeeping and conforming points | Various |

---

## II. Issues, in Priority Order

### Issue 1 (HIGH): Buyer's objection to Supplement No. 1 was late, so the Calloway odometer class action may be deemed accepted and cured

**Where it appears**
- SPA §6.8 (Disclosure Schedule Supplements)
- Disclosure Schedule, Supplement No. 1, cover statement
- Buyer's objection letter dated September 29, 2026

**What the documents say**
- **The deemed-acceptance rule.** Under SPA §6.8, a Schedule Supplement is **"deemed accepted by Buyer"** unless Buyer delivers a written objection "within ten (10) Business Days after receipt." A deemed-accepted supplement cures the related breach for two purposes:
  - the Buyer closing conditions in §8.2; and
  - **indemnification under Article IX**.
- **Delivery date.** The Supplement No. 1 cover statement says it was delivered to Buyer **on September 8, 2026** (a Tuesday) by email to Buyer's notice address under §11.3, with a courier copy.
- **What the supplement adds.** It discloses the *Calloway Pre-Owned Motors v. Stonebarrow* putative nationwide class action (S.D.N.Y.). The claims are under the federal Odometer Act and N.Y. GBL §349. The plaintiff seeks the greater of treble damages or $10,000 per violation, covering vehicles sold since January 2023. The supplement schedules the action against §§4.13, 4.5 and 4.10.
- **The deadline.** Counting ten Business Days from September 8 (Labor Day was September 7, the day before) gives these days: Sept. 9, 10, 11, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 21 and 22. **The objection window closed on September 22, 2026.**
- **The objection.** Vailous's letter is dated **September 29, 2026**, which is **five Business Days late**.

**Why it matters for Vailous**
- **Indemnity.** Seller has a straightforward argument that the Calloway Action is deemed accepted. If so, it cures any breach of §4.10 (Title and Odometer Compliance), §4.13 (Litigation) and §4.5 (Undisclosed Liabilities) for indemnity purposes.
- **Closing conditions.** Seller can also argue that the Calloway Action cannot be used to show that the §8.2(a) bring-down condition has failed. That weakens Buyer's ability to refuse to close or to terminate under §10.1(c).
- **Size of the exposure.** Statutory damages of $10,000 per violation across a nationwide class of auction purchases since 2023 could reach the eight-figure range. That is far above both the $3,150,000 escrow and the $4,200,000 general cap.
- **Arguments still open to Buyer.** The September 29 letter disputes the supplement and reserves rights, so Buyer has not conceded the point. Its main substantive argument is in letter ¶3(a): §6.8 reaches only matters "arising or first becoming known to Seller after the date of this Agreement," and the alleged conduct dates to January 2023, well before signing. That argument has some force, but it is a litigation position. It is not a dependable protection.
- **A partial backstop.** SPA §9.2(d) gives a specific indemnity for Title and Odometer Losses on pre-Closing vehicles "regardless of whether disclosed in the Disclosure Schedule," and Buyer's letter relies on it (¶4(a)). This is helpful. However, Seller can still invoke deemed acceptance to cut off the §4.10, §4.13 and §4.5 representation claims and the closing-condition argument. We should not rely on §9.2(d) alone.

**Recommended fix (before Closing)**
1. **Get a written waiver from Seller.** Seller should waive the deemed-acceptance and cure effect of §6.8 for Supplement No. 1, in a writing signed under SPA §11.7, either standalone or in an SPA amendment. It should confirm that the Calloway Action does not cure any breach for purposes of §8.2 or Article IX.
2. **Add a specific, uncapped, line-item indemnity for the Calloway Action.** It should cover all Losses from the Calloway Action and the underlying conduct, including defense costs, settlement and any regulatory follow-on. It should:
   - be expressly outside the §9.5(a) basket and cap;
   - survive until the action is finally resolved plus 60 days; and
   - be backed by a separate special escrow or holdback. One option is to enlarge the Indemnity Escrow Amount, as letter ¶7 already suggests.
3. **Add a pre-Closing control covenant.** Seller should be barred from settling the Calloway Action, consenting to judgment or stipulating to class certification without Buyer's consent. Buyer should also have consultation rights on the October 22 response and on later filings. The letter asked for this under §6.1, but it should be made a binding covenant.
4. **Fallback.** If Seller refuses, Buyer should preserve the position that the §6.8 supplement right does not reach pre-signing conduct. Buyer should then weigh whether to close by the Outside Date at all.
5. **Going forward.** Calendar the §6.8 deadline for any further Schedule Supplement on the day it is received.

---

### Issue 2 (HIGH): General Representations survive only 90 days after Closing

**Where it appears**
- SPA §9.1 (Survival)
- SPA §1.1 (definition of "Escrow Release Date")
- Escrow Agreement §4.1

**What the documents say**
- **Survival.** SPA §9.1 provides that the General Representations "shall survive the Closing **until the Escrow Release Date**." The General Representations include:
  - financial statements (§4.4)
  - undisclosed liabilities (§4.5)
  - consignor trust funds (§4.6)
  - dealer and auction licenses (§4.7)
  - auction receivables (§4.8)
  - floorplan arrangements (§4.9)
  - title and odometer compliance (§4.10)
  - material contracts (§4.11)
  - litigation (§4.13)
- **The borrowed definition.** The SPA does not define the Escrow Release Date itself. §1.1 imports the Escrow Agreement's definition. Escrow Agreement §4.1 then sets it as "the date that is **ninety (90) days after the Closing Date**."
- **Release mechanics.** Escrow Agreement §§4.2 and 5.1 release the escrow on that date. Only claims noticed by then are held back.

**Why it matters for Vailous**
- **The window is about 90 days.** Read together, these provisions give Buyer roughly 90 days after Closing to assert any claim for breach of the General Representations. After that, the general indemnity, the $4,200,000 cap and the $3,150,000 escrow are effectively gone.
- **That is too short for this business.** The problems most likely to surface in an auction business usually appear months after Closing. Examples include:
  - consignor-fund shortfalls or commingling;
  - uncollectible dealer and floorplan receivables;
  - license or bond problems in NY, NJ, PA or CT;
  - errors in the financial statements.

  The first post-Closing audit cycle will not be finished within 90 days.
- **The timing overlaps with the price adjustment.** The §2.4 post-closing statement is itself due 90 days after Closing. In practice, Buyer would be preparing the working-capital true-up at the same moment its indemnity window closes.
- **The precedence clause does not help.** There is no conflict between the documents: the SPA deliberately adopts the Escrow Agreement's date, so SPA §11.12 has nothing to resolve.

**Recommended fix (before Closing)**
1. Amend SPA §9.1 so that the General Representations survive for a **stand-alone period of at least 15 to 18 months** after Closing. The period should not be tied to the escrow definition.
2. Amend Escrow Agreement §4.1 so that the Escrow Release Date **matches** that survival period. Consider a staged release, such as 50% at 12 months and the balance at 18 months, net of pending claims.
3. Make clear that claims noticed in good faith before the survival period expires survive until resolved. §9.1 already says this; it should be confirmed in the Escrow Agreement claim-notice mechanics in §5.1.

### Issue 3 (HIGH): Seller Note chooses Delaware law and forum, against the SPA's New York choices; the precedence clause does not reach the Note

**Where it appears**
- Seller Note §8.1 and §8.2
- SPA §9.7 (Right of Setoff)
- SPA §11.8 (Governing Law), §11.9 (Jurisdiction) and §11.12 (Order of Precedence)

**What the documents say**
- **The SPA.** It is governed by **New York law** (§11.8), with **exclusive jurisdiction in state or federal courts in New York County** (§11.9).
- **The setoff right.** SPA §9.7 lets Buyer **set off** indemnifiable Losses "against any **payments due under the Seller Note**." It also provides that a good-faith setoff is not a default under the Note.
- **The Note.** Seller Note §8.1 selects **"the laws of the State of Delaware,"** and §8.2 requires that any proceeding "arising out of or relating to this Note" be brought **exclusively in "the courts of the State of Delaware"** in New Castle County, or the District of Delaware.
- **No express setoff in the Note.** The Note does not mention Buyer's setoff right. The only payment default under §6.1(a) is a failure to pay when due after a ten-Business-Day notice.
- **No precedence cure.** SPA §11.12 makes the SPA prevail only over the "Ancillary Agreements." That term is a closed list of the Escrow Agreement, TSA, IP Assignment Agreement and Bill of Sale. **The Seller Note is not included**, so the precedence clause does **not** resolve this conflict.

**Why it matters for Vailous**
- **The Note is Buyer's main post-Closing protection.** The $6,000,000 Seller Note is Buyer's most practical source of recovery after Closing, especially once the escrow is released.
- **How a dispute would likely unfold.** If Buyer withholds a Note payment as a setoff, Pritouth would likely sue on the Note in Delaware. It would argue that:
  - the Note is a self-contained instrument governed by Delaware law;
  - Delaware is the exclusive forum; and
  - the Note itself contains no setoff defense.
- **The resulting problem.** Buyer's defense depends on New York-law indemnity rights that must be litigated exclusively in New York County. The likely result is parallel proceedings, inconsistent rulings, a fight over which forum clause controls, and a risk of acceleration under Note §6.2 and fee-shifting under §6.3. The protection the setoff was meant to give, namely holding back deferred price against indemnity claims, is seriously weakened.

**Recommended fix (before Closing; the Note is still an agreed form and has not been issued)**
1. **Conform the Note** to New York law and the exclusive New York County forum, matching SPA §§11.8 and 11.9. This is the cleanest fix.
2. **Add an express setoff clause to the Note.** It should state that:
   - payments are subject to Buyer's setoff rights under SPA §9.7;
   - a good-faith setoff is not an Event of Default and does not trigger default interest or acceleration; and
   - any dispute over a setoff is resolved under the SPA's dispute provisions.
3. **Belt and braces.** Add the Seller Note to the "Ancillary Agreements" definition in SPA §1.1 and to the list in §11.12, so the SPA prevails if any inconsistency remains.
4. **Coordinate with the lender.** Confirm that any Subordination Agreement under Note §5.1 does not override or limit the setoff right.

### Issue 4 (MEDIUM): Pritouth may assign or delegate the TSA to anyone, including a competitor

**Where it appears**
- TSA §13.3 (Assignment and Delegation)

**What the document says**
- **Provider's rights.** TSA §13.3 allows Provider (Pritouth) to "assign this Agreement, or delegate or subcontract the performance of any Services, in whole or in part, **to any Person without the consent of Recipient**."
- **Recipient's restriction.** The Company, by contrast, may not assign without Pritouth's consent.

**Why it matters for Vailous**
- **The services involve sensitive data and systems.** Under Schedule A, Pritouth will run several core functions, each with access to the Company's most sensitive data and systems:
  - the Company's title office (title files and odometer statements);
  - TitleTrack hosting;
  - accounting, including daily reconciliation of the Consignor Funds trust accounts; and
  - LaneLink and simulcast systems, including access management for consignor and bidder accounts.
- **Who could end up performing them.** Under §13.3, Pritouth could hand these functions, and the access that comes with them, to a **competing wholesale auction operator** or to an unvetted offshore subcontractor. The Company would have no say.
- **Existing protections are weak in practice.** The non-compete in SPA §6.6 binds only Seller and its Affiliates, and it expressly carves out performance of the Services. The data-use limits in TSA §7.1 bind Provider, but Buyer would be left enforcing them after the fact against an assignee it did not choose.
- **Licensing risk.** Title and odometer functions are performed under the Company's state Licenses (TSA §3.2). A poorly performing delegate creates regulatory risk that sits with the Company as licensee of record.

**Recommended fix (before Closing)**
1. Make assignment **mutual-consent**. Provider may not assign, delegate or subcontract without Recipient's prior written consent. Consent may be withheld in Recipient's sole discretion for title, odometer, consignor-fund and data-access functions.
2. Add an **express bar on any assignment, delegation or subcontracting to a Person engaged in wholesale vehicle auctions or remarketing**, or to an Affiliate of such a Person.
3. Make Provider **remain fully liable** for any permitted subcontractor. Flow down the obligations in §7 (data and confidentiality) and §3.2 (licensed functions).
4. Give Recipient a **termination right with migration assistance** if Provider undergoes a change of control to a competitor.
